explanations.explanation: Verse 7 answers the question right away: “Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.” The one coming up from the wilderness is described “…like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense…” (Song of Solomon 3:6). Solomon is Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1). Smoke and spices. That's an entrance, friend.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, did send chariots out once, in Exodus 14:7. But that's a different story in a different book. In this poem, the smoke and spices belong to Solomon's carriage (Song of Solomon 3:7). Good guess for a dramatic entrance, though.

Naaman, an Aram army commander (2 Kings 5:1), did show up with horses and chariots in 2 Kings 5:9. He just isn't in this poem. The writer says this one is Solomon's carriage. I'd love to tell you Naaman smelled like myrrh, but the text doesn't say that.

Twelve is a nice number, but it's not the one in the text. The poem says the carriage is escorted by “…sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.” Twelve would be a small crew. Sixty is a whole parade of bodyguards.
It's sixty. The poem says the carriage is escorted by “…sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.” That's a lot of swords walking beside one carriage. I'd feel very safe, and very watched.

The text says each man has his sword at his side, “…prepared for the terror of the night.” These men are skilled with the sword and experienced in warfare. So when the lights go out, they're ready. I wouldn't want to be whatever the night is sending.

Sunrise is a fine time to be ready, but it's not what the poem names. These warriors are “…prepared for the terror of the night.” The text doesn't mention a morning attack. Their swords are at their sides, and the night is the thing the poem names.

The poem never mentions a call to battle. It says each man has his sword at his side, “…prepared for the terror of the night.” They're also described as skilled with the sword and experienced in warfare. That's the readiness the text gives.

explanations.answer: Love from the daughters of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The poem says the interior is “…inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” The posts are silver, the base is gold and the seat is purple fabric, but the inside gets something better. Fancy wood is nice. That's nicer.

explanations.answer: Gold from the land of Ophir
explanations.explanation: Gold sounds right for Solomon, but the poem puts gold in the base. The inside is “…inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” Ophir isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The inlay is something you can't buy.

explanations.answer: Ivory from the ships of Tarshish
explanations.explanation: Ivory would look sharp, but it's not in this poem. The interior is “…inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” The carriage already has silver posts, a gold base and a purple seat. The inside gets something no merchant sells.

The poem says, “Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon…” They're invited to look at the king in his crown. The text says it's the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding. Big day, friend.

The elders aren't called in this verse. The call is “Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon…” If you picked the elders, I get it, because they sound like official guests. This guest list just reads differently.
No priests in this verse. The call is “Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon…” The poem doesn't mention a temple here at all. The ones called to gaze are the daughters of Zion.

That's it. The verse says Solomon wears “…the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding…” His mother is the one placing it on his head. A king's mother crowning him on his wedding day is a proud moment.

Victory is a reasonable guess for a king with sixty warriors around him. But the verse says the crown came “…on the day of his wedding…” His mother crowned him then. The poem doesn't mention a battle here.

A crown on a newborn would be a lot of hat. The poem says his mother crowned him “…on the day of his wedding—the day of his heart’s rejoicing.” So this is a grown man on a very happy day. No baby involved.
Nobody's missing in this picture. The verse says, “each has its twin, and not one of them is lost.” Every single sheep is there, matched up in pairs. A complete set, with nobody left behind.

That's right, none are missing. The groom says her teeth are like newly shorn sheep coming up from the washing, and “each has its twin, and not one of them is lost.” It's a picture of a full, matched set. I'd call that a perfect count.

Yes, the groom says her neck is like “…the tower of David, built with rows of stones…” A thousand shields of warriors hang on it. David is Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and his tower is a strong, proud picture. He is saying something grand about her.

An altar is a strong picture, but it's not the one in the verse. The groom says her neck is like “…the tower of David, built with rows of stones…” A thousand warriors' shields hang on it. The text doesn't use an altar here.
The picture is smaller than a city, but still mighty. The verse says “…the tower of David, built with rows of stones…” A thousand shields of warriors hang on it. The text names a tower, not a city.

Yes. After picture after picture, he says, “You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.” He doesn't pick out one part. He says all of her. That's a man with only good things to say.

The text says the opposite. In verse 7 he says, “You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.” No flaw at all. He's been describing her one picture at a time, and here he says it of all of her.

Dens of lions and mountains of leopards don't sound like a vacation spot. The groom says, “Come with me from Lebanon, my bride…” and calls her down from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards. I think he wants her out of that rough country and beside him. I'd take that invitation too.
Nothing in this verse is crowded. He calls her down from “…the dens of the lions…” and “…the mountains of the leopards.” Those sound wild, not busy. A crowd I could handle. A leopard, not so much.

The verse doesn't call these places holy. It names the peak of Amana, the summits of Senir and Hermon, “…the dens of the lions…” and “…the mountains of the leopards.” Lions and leopards give it a wild, dangerous feel. I think he's calling her out of that.

Yes, he says, “you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck.” One glance. That's all it took. Me, I smell one fresh batch coming out of the oven and I'm done for.
The text says it. He tells her, “you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck.” So one glance did it. His heart was gone in a moment.
It's the other way around. The groom says, “Your love is much better than wine…” He even adds that the fragrance of her perfume beats all spices. Her love comes out on top.

Right, wine loses. He says, “How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine…” Her love comes out ahead of wine, and her perfume beats all spices. In this poem, her love wins.

This garden has a lock. The groom says, “…you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.” That's not a garden for anyone who wanders in. Locked, enclosed, sealed. Three ways of saying the same thing.

Right, it's closed up. He says, “My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.” A locked garden isn't open to just anyone. The poem says it three different ways.

That's the one. The verse says, “You are a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon.” Lebanon has been in the poem before, in his call to come with him from there. Now fresh water pours down from it.

Zion is in this passage, since the daughters of Zion were called out to see the king. But the well of fresh water comes “…flowing down from Lebanon.” That's how the verse ends. Zion is a nice guess, but the text says Lebanon.
Carmel isn't named anywhere in this passage. The verse says the well of fresh water is “…flowing down from Lebanon.” He's used Lebanon before, so the water pours from a place he's already mentioned.

Yes, the call is “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices.” Both winds are called to breathe on the garden. That garden is full of spices, and the winds are asked to spread the fragrance.

Rain would water a garden, but the poem calls for something else. The call is “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind.” They're asked to breathe on the garden and spread its fragrance. Wind carries scent, and that's what this verse needs.

Dew isn't in this verse. The call is “Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind.” The winds are called to breathe on the garden and spread the fragrance of its spices. That's wind work, not dew work.

The same call says, “Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.” The beloved is the one invited in. The garden was described as locked up in verse 12, so this invitation matters. The beloved is the one asked to taste the choicest fruits.

No watchmen in this stretch of the poem. The invitation is for “my beloved,” to come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits. The garden has been described as locked up, so I'd say it's a very particular guest list.

No shepherds in this passage, friend. The sheep in 4:2 are a picture used for teeth, not a flock anybody is tending. The verse says, “Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.” Then 5:1 says, “I have come to my garden…”
Yes, the groom says, “I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride…” That comes in 5:1, right after the call in 4:16. The call went out, and he says he has come.
The text says he did. Right after the invitation in 4:16, he says, “I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride…” The arrival comes in the very next verse. That's the groom's own word on it.
That's the line in 5:1: “Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.” The friends are told to eat and drink, and the second part says to drink freely. When a verse says eat, I'm listening.

Singing and dancing would fit a party, but that's not what the verse says. The voice tells the friends, “Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.” Eating and drinking is what the voice asks. I can always dance later.
No waiting in this verse. The voice says, “Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.” The friends are told to eat and drink. That's the instruction, and nothing in it says to watch.
